title: FormData & File Uploads
subtitle: Uploading files with FormData, multipart/form-data, progress tracking, and drag-and-drop
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: JSON can't represent binary data (images, PDFs, videos). File uploads require a different content type — multipart/form-data — that supports mixing text fields and binary file data in one request body.
whyItExists.solution: FormData builds multipart/form-data bodies automatically. Pass it directly to fetch() — don't set Content-Type (the browser sets it with the boundary string). For progress tracking, use XMLHttpRequest's upload.onprogress instead of fetch().
whyItExists.whenToUse: Profile picture upload, document attachment, bulk import (CSV), any form with a file input.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: For small amounts of binary data that can be base64-encoded, a JSON body with a base64 field is simpler. For very large files (>100MB), use presigned URLs (upload directly to S3/GCS from the browser).

explainModes.beginner: To upload a file, you use FormData. It's like a form in JavaScript — you append fields to it: fd.append('file', theFile). Then you pass fd to fetch() as the body, without setting Content-Type (the browser handles that). The server receives it as a multipart form upload — same format as an HTML <form> with enctype='multipart/form-data'.
explainModes.simple: const fd = new FormData(); fd.append('file', fileInput.files[0]); fd.append('description', 'my photo'). fetch('/upload', { method: 'POST', body: fd }). Do NOT set Content-Type header — let the browser set multipart/form-data; boundary=... automatically. Input file via HTML: <input type='file'>. Drag-and-drop: event.dataTransfer.files[0]. Multiple files: fd.append('files', file) multiple times or fileInput.multiple = true.
explainModes.standard: Progress tracking: fetch() doesn't expose upload progress — use XMLHttpRequest instead. xhr.upload.onprogress = (e) => { const pct = (e.loaded / e.total * 100).toFixed(1) }. Multiple files: Array.from(fileInput.files).forEach(f => fd.append('files', f)). File validation before upload: check file.type (MIME type), file.size, file.name extension. Creating thumbnails: URL.createObjectURL(file) — local preview URL, revoke with URL.revokeObjectURL() after use. Presigned URLs: for large files, backend generates a presigned S3 URL — frontend uploads directly to S3, bypassing your server entirely.
explainModes.technical: multipart/form-data format: boundary string separates parts. Each part has headers (Content-Disposition with name/filename, Content-Type for files) and body (text or binary). Server parsing: express with multer: upload.single('file') puts file in req.file — { fieldname, originalname, mimetype, size, buffer/path }. Streaming uploads: for very large files, pipe the ReadableStream to avoid buffering the whole file in memory. TransformStream: compress before upload. File chunks: split into 5MB chunks and upload in parallel — reassemble on server. Resume interrupted uploads: TUS protocol.
explainModes.deepDive: Presigned URL flow: frontend → backend: 'I want to upload a 50MB video'. Backend → S3: 'generate a URL valid for 15 minutes for this key'. Backend → frontend: presigned URL. Frontend → S3: PUT directly with the presigned URL. Benefits: doesn't go through your server (saves egress costs, no timeout issues), S3 handles chunking and resumability natively. S3 multipart upload API: split into 5MB+ parts, upload in parallel with Part numbers, call CompleteMultipartUpload. Signed URL alternative: Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob SAS URLs — same concept. Virus scanning: scan uploaded files before making them accessible — ClamAV, AWS Security Hub, or dedicated services.

content.text: Never set Content-Type manually for FormData. The boundary string (e.g. `boundary=----WebKitFormBoundary...`) is auto-generated — if you override Content-Type, the server can't parse the file and the upload fails.

questions.question: Why use XMLHttpRequest instead of fetch() when you need to track upload progress?
options: fetch() can't upload files at all
The fetch() API doesn't expose upload progress events. XMLHttpRequest has an upload.onprogress event that fires as bytes are sent, enabling a progress bar.
XMLHttpRequest is faster than fetch() for large files
fetch() has a 10MB file size limit
questions.explanation: fetch() returns a Response only when the request is complete — there's no way to observe bytes being uploaded. XMLHttpRequest's xhr.upload.onprogress fires repeatedly with { loaded, total } as the upload proceeds. This is the only way to show a progress bar for uploads. For downloads, you CAN track progress with fetch() using response.body.getReader() to read the stream chunk by chunk.

faq.q: How do I upload large files without hitting server limits or timeouts?
faq.a: Use presigned URLs (S3, GCS, Azure Blob). Flow: (1) Frontend asks your backend 'I want to upload a 200MB video'. (2) Your backend calls AWS S3 to generate a presigned URL valid for 15 minutes. (3) Your backend returns the URL to the frontend. (4) Frontend uses fetch() or XMLHttpRequest to PUT the file directly to S3 — no traffic goes through your server. Benefits: no server timeout, no 100MB body limit, bandwidth goes directly to S3. S3 also supports multipart uploads (split into 5MB+ chunks, upload in parallel, reassemble).

examples: Cloudinary — presigned upload URL flow for images/videos
GitHub — file attachment in issues uses multipart form upload
Google Drive — chunked upload API for files >5MB
